**Diary of Mr. Richard Reade – 12th March, 1874**

Today I set out from Tunis with Captain Balfour, our guide and the only other Englishman in the expedition. We were escorted by the “Bey of the Camp,” Sidi Mohammed, who rode a beautiful bay charger and led a procession of Mamelukes, Turkish infantry, and spahis. The plain of Manouba stretched before us, a vast expanse of salt‑crusted earth that glittered like a field of stars. We crossed the running stream Zebharah, where an ancient bridge once stood; the new one was in fine repair, a testament to the ingenuity of the local engineers.

Our first major stop was **Kairwan**. The town lay on the edge of the Sahara, its walls a patchwork of mud‑brick and stone. We were received by the Kaed of the Jereed, a man named Braun, and a small contingent of Arab guards. The air was hot, but the shade of the palm groves offered relief. We met the famed saint Sidi Amour Abeda, whose reputation for miracles was well known. He welcomed us with a simple meal of dates and kouskousou, and his presence reminded me of the spiritual depth that permeates this land.

The landscape around Kairwan is a paradox: a barren salt plain interrupted by sudden, lush oases. We saw gazelles darting across the dunes, their speed rivaling that of a greyhound, and a flock of Kader birds—small, partridge‑sized, yet fierce. The Turkish infantry, though irregular, marched with a disciplined vigor that impressed even Captain Balfour.

Our journey continued toward Ghafsa, where we crossed a shallow stream that ran through a valley of reeds. The water was cool and refreshing, a welcome contrast to the relentless sun. We paused to observe a group of snakes slithering along the banks, their scales glinting in the afternoon light.

Throughout the expedition, the diversity of peoples—Mamelukes, Turkish soldiers, Arab guards, and the local Berber tribes—has been striking. Each group carries its own customs and stories, yet all share a common respect for the land and its people. Captain Balfour, ever the gentleman, has been a steady companion, his observations of the terrain and the people as keen as my own.

I am struck by the resilience of the inhabitants, who thrive in a region where the soil is rich in salt and nitrous efflorescence, yet receives little manure. Their agriculture, especially the cultivation of dates in the Jereed, is a marvel of irrigation and patience.

As the sun set over the dunes, I felt a profound sense of awe. North Africa is a land of contrasts—of salt and water, of desert and oasis, of ancient traditions and modern ambitions. I look forward to the next day's adventures, confident that each step will reveal more of this remarkable region.

The sun was high when we crossed the great expanse that is Kairwan, a town that lies at the edge of the desert and the sea. The air was dry, the ground cracked, and the horizon seemed to stretch forever. The people we met were as varied as the landscape. We were welcomed by the local Bey of the Camp, Sidi Mohammed, who greeted us with a salute from the guns—one of the shots nearly struck Captain Balfour’s head! We also encountered the Mamelukes of the Seraglio, superbly mounted and proud, and the Boabs, who guarded the Bey’s tent with a solemn vigilance. The diversity of peoples—Moorish villagers, French spies, and the occasional snake-charming tribesman—made the journey all the more fascinating. The landscape itself was a tapestry of gazelles darting across the plain, partridges flitting through the reeds, and the occasional sight of a hare or a bird called Kader.

Despite the hardships of the march, the camaraderie among the officers and the sheer beauty of the North African plains made the day memorable. I look forward to the next leg of our journey, hoping to learn more about the customs and geography of this vast and varied land.

In late August 1864, a sudden and violent uprising by the Sioux erupted along the Minnesota frontier. Following the battle, General Pope telegraphed the War Department that the Indian war was over and requested disposition of his troops.
